Doctors warn that such life-threatening cases are becoming more common.
For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way.
But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it’s primarily used to beef up cows.
Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week’s issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like.
“Use of AAS has now become a major international substance use disorder,” they wrote. In the US, it’s estimated that between 2.9 and 4 million people, mostly male athletes, use AAS. To put this in a public health perspective, this is more than the number of people in the US with an HIV infection.
“Clinicians should be prepared to encounter increasing numbers of patients presenting with the long-term effects of AAS exposure, including cardiomyopathy, atherosclerotic disease, and anabolic steroid–induced hypogonadism.”
Patients also need to be prepared for what recovery looks like, which they described as being “lengthy and varied.” The man’s case offers a stark example.
The problems started when he was 39. He fell ill after returning from a trip to the Caribbean and went to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston with a fever, chills, and trouble breathing. Tests suggested he had an acute kidney injury, liver damage, and an injured heart. Testing of his heart showed that the left chamber was pumping out just 21 percent of its blood in a beat (a normal amount is above 50 percent). His heart only got worse from there, and within hours, he ended up on a type of life support called ECMO (venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation), a machine that does the work of both the heart and lungs in dire circumstances. He luckily recovered—and quickly. But doctors were baffled by the cause.
When he was weaned off ECMO a few days later, his heart function normalized. Doctors looked for evidence of anything that could have sparked the sudden cardiac spiral. They found nothing but a mildly elevated level of antibodies against a toxin made by Streptococcus bacteria. In rare instances, an infection with these germs can lead to a condition called poststreptococcal myocarditis, which could potentially explain some of his symptoms. It was their best guess. They prescribed him antibiotics, as well as drugs to lower his blood pressure.
Two years later, he went to another hospital. This time it was for acute pain in his abdomen and legs. Doctors found signs of cell death in his kidneys. The arteries that supply blood to his kidneys appeared narrowed, suggesting a condition called renal-artery stenosis. There were also signs of inflammation in his blood vessels. But the doctors at the hospital couldn’t pinpoint the problem. They prescribed him anti-inflammatory drugs and sent him on his way.
For the next five years, the man started seeing a cadre of specialists to monitor his health, including doctors in primary care, cardiology, nephrology, rheumatology, general medicine, sleep medicine, and psychiatry. When he was about 46, he reported fatigue to his primary care doctor, who found that his testosterone level was low. The man then went to an endocrinologist, reporting not just fatigue but low libido and poor sleep. The endocrinologist recommended treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, which can increase the risk of low testosterone.
A year later, the man added a hematologist to his rotation of care providers. A routine blood test revealed abnormally high levels of red blood cells (erythrocytosis). The hematologist noted the man also had high blood pressure (150/108 mm Hg) but found everything else to be normal. The hematologist ended up attributing the erythrocytosis to the man’s sleep apnea and renal-artery stenosis.
It wasn’t until he arrived again at Mass General in 2026 that doctors finally put it all together. Now 50, the man was once again experiencing heart failure—and he had again just returned from the Caribbean.
In the case report, doctors provided a more complete picture of the man, noting that he lived with his wife and children in eastern Massachusetts, worked as a facilities manager, and described himself as a workout “fanatic.” He used tanning beds and applied spray tans. He told doctors he had erectile dysfunction and reduced libido for several years. They also noticed that he had mildly enlarged breast tissue (a condition called gynecomastia), progressive insulin resistance, decreased levels of “good” cholesterol (HDL or high-density lipoprotein), and fatty liver disease.
When he arrived at the hospital, he reported five days of worsening chest tightness and pressure, fatigue, swelling in his legs, and trouble breathing. His heart was racing at 134 beats per minute. His blood pressure was high at 146/106 mm Hg. Doctors described him as “muscular, tanned, anxious, and in mild distress.” Tests showed his heart was once again failing, with the left chamber pumping out just 20 percent of its blood.
The doctors started reviewing a long list of possible explanations. They ruled out infectious diseases that can cause heart inflammation (myocarditis), as well as autoimmune conditions, medication side effects, and toxins. The explanation they were left with—which also seemed to explain much of his other problems—was high doses of testosterone, or perhaps an AAS.
Illicit use of AAS is clearly linked to the heart problems, including the decreased blood pumping the man had, as well as strain and damage. It could also explain his enlarged breast tissue, fatty liver and signs of liver damage, progressive insulin resistance, kidney injuries, high blood pressure, and high levels of red blood cells (erythrocytosis). The sleep problems, fatigue, and low testosterone levels—which doctors previously guessed were from obstructive sleep apnea—could actually be from a drop in natural hormone production after doses of AAS (a condition called hypogonadism).
In the man’s lengthy medical history, he had never mentioned using AAS or testosterone supplements. Doctors prepared to have a delicate conversation to determine if he was secretly using the drugs. When they finally broached the topic, he confessed; he had been intermittently using high doses of AAS to boost his muscles, taking the most recent dose before his vacation to the Caribbean. The testosterone derivative he used was trenbolone, an AAS only approved for use in veterinary medicine; it’s mostly used in livestock.
The doctors then tested his total testosterone level, finding it was so high that the test couldn’t accurately measure it. The assay’s range of detection was 12 to 1,500 nanograms per deciliter of blood. His level was over 1,500 ng/dl. The range considered normal for the test was between 249 and 836 ng/dl. The doctors gave their final diagnosis: androgen excess–related cardiomyopathy.
The primary treatment for his heart is to stop taking AAS. Doctors prescribed him medications for high blood pressure, heart failure, and diabetes. Four months later, heart tests showed his left chamber was pumping 49 percent of its blood, a significant improvement. The state of his liver also improved. But recovery from the AAS-induced hypogonadism was a much longer, more difficult journey. It was made harder because he was over age 35, had taken AAS for more than a decade, and had preexisting dysfunction.

AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run.
An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures.
Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it.
Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it:
You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0.
It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun , and opens the console in your browser.
Add one model key. In the console, set a password, then add a key under Settings → Model keys . One OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode.
Run your first agent. Open Templates , apply KYB due diligence , and start a run with a company's name and website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's Report tab has a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's Learning tab to see what it kept for next time.
Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me .
If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use, which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files, but get no shell.
Want your own server with a URL? Deploy it to Render in one click.
Workflows that make the call. A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route. Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review.
Every agent in one place. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool.
Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code.
You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer.
Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. AgentRun checks it, grades it, and commits the keepers to the agent's own git folder. The next run starts from there.
The agent's Learning tab shows every note, skill and workflow and the log of changes, and each run shows which notes it was given and opened. Retire anything there, or with npx @parcha/agentrun learning retire and the note's ETag. Git keeps the history, so a retired note can come back.
Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, main . A run reads the index of active notes in its instructions and gets the learned skills beside its own. Code checks every proposal first. An item that breaks a rule of its own (a size or count limit, its name, its shape) is left out and the rest goes on. A secret or a hidden character anywhere in the answer, a file outside the folder, a deletion or a full index drops the whole answer, since no item of it can be trusted. Then one grader judges what it says, and AgentRun commits what passes. A risky rule waits for your OK. A rule the run found in a page or a pasted email, or a note that holds an account number, is dropped.
Once an agent's notes outgrow the learning budget, each run gets the ones that bear on its first message, whole, and a line for each of the rest. A run that only ran a learned workflow isn't asked what to keep.
A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a trigger can start one.
An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs , not a recording of a model run.
Watch any workflow run node by node, pause it and resume it, and read every decision and why it was made:
Steps can call tools, run a model, ask a fast typed question, branch on the answer, map over a list in parallel, loop a bounded number of times, call other workflows, or hand the hard case to an agent. Save one as an agent's workflow field; npx @parcha/agentrun workflows validate checks it first. The workflow language also runs on its own inside your app, with a TypeScript builder .
Every agent, revision, run and step lives in one store. Stop the server mid-run and start it again, and the run carries on. With several runners, another runner picks up a dead runner's runs once their 30-second lease runs out. A finished step is never run again; a write a crash cut off mid-call is marked interrupted rather than retried, so you can check it.
Five ready-made agents. Apply one in one screen, make it yours, and measure it with its own eval cases. Each template is one folder: the agent's instructions, its skills, its rules and its eval cases. Templates → Apply grants nothing until you tick each MCP tool yourself.
npx @parcha/agentrun template eval DIR runs a template's eval cases as real runs on a throwaway server and grades them. Template packages has the folder format.
Triggers start capped runs on their own: schedules, signed webhooks and GitHub pull request events.
Harnesses. Name one in the agent's definition with harness . Approvals, caps, computers, triggers and learning work the same on each. npx @parcha/agentrun server capabilities says which harnesses your server runs.
Computers. An agent gets a computer with one setting. It gets the tools for that kind and nothing else, and changing the computer changes nothing else about the agent.
Every kind but none names its provider. An agent with no computer setting gets the Docker sandbox where the server has Docker, and no computer otherwise. Remote computers bill through your own account with the vendor.
@parcha/agentrun-computer is the protocol underneath: one small daemon in every computer and one provider per vendor.
npx @parcha/agentrun is also the server's CLI. Run these in a second terminal while the server is up; the CLI finds it and its token by itself. The script makes an agent, starts a run capped at $1, lets the agent ask you a question, answers it, and reads the file the agent wrote. With Docker on, the first run waits for the sandbox image.
runs wait exits 0 when the run completed, 1 when it failed, and 8 when it waits on you: a question, its cap, or an approval. runs timeline RUN_ID --follow streams each step as it happens, and every run carries a console_url to its page. npx @parcha/agentrun help lists every command; npx @parcha/agentrun skill install --claude (or --codex ) teaches your coding agent the CLI.
With the TypeScript client ( npm install @parcha/agentrun-client , no dependencies). The client reads its server and token from the environment; the server prints both when it starts (with npx @parcha/agentrun , the token is in ~/.agentrun/.token , and the address is normally http://127.0.0.1:7340 ):

The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own tits own models.
Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.
Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.
Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.
The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.
That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.
Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.

During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit.
Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a “simple” rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, “the best part is no part.” Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket’s development cycle.
“Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines,” he said of the rocket. “So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite.”
I am not a rocket engineer, and I am not mad at Avellan. But he sure seems to be substantially underestimating the challenge of building rockets.
Avellan also has a problem. AST SpaceMobile appears to be successful in building very large satellites, Bluebirds, that are capable of providing direct-to-cell capability from an orbit about 550km above Earth. The problem is there is a commercial launch crunch, and the company is struggling to get its satellites on orbit today, and projects to do so into the future.
“We’re not doing this thing because we like rockets,” he said during the presentation. “We’re not doing this thing because we want to be in the launch business. We want this because we have so much demand of our satellites, and as you have seen it, we cannot get enough launches.”
The Blacklift rocket will be “simple,” he said, because it will be solely tailored to lift five Bluebird satellites into low-Earth orbit at a time. It will have 20 metric tons of lift capacity, a reusable first stage, and launch twice a month from a pad at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia that formerly served the Antares rocket. It will have all composite tanks and three stages. And, Avellan said, it will be ready to launch in 2028.
However, Avellan believes AST has a workaround: It is committed to spending $1.3 billion to acquire enough engines for the first three Blacklift launches from Firefly Aerospace, as well as a license to manufacture additional engines over time. He is basing this argument on the Miranda first stage engine, which he said is “ready to fly.”
But that’s not quite true. However, Miranda has not yet completed its formal qualification campaign, much less flown on an orbital rocket. Firefly chief executive Jason Kim said this week that qualification testing remains underway. Moreover, little is known publicly about the readiness of the upper stage engine, Vira, that AST is also acquiring from Firefly for its rocket.
Another questionable assertion is Avellan’s statement that 80 percent of a rocket’s design cycle is due to engine development. “I mean, that has been proven,” he said.
I’m not sure it has. Propulsion is definitely one of the most challenging aspects of developing a rocket.
However, Rocket Lab, which has considerably more experience building orbital rockets than AST, has suffered two significant setbacks this year involving Neutron’s composite propellant tanks. These structures, as well as flight software, avionics, stage separation, payload fairings, qualification testing, and so much more, can lead to significant delays in the development of a rocket. And then there are the equally difficult challenges of scaling from development to production at rate, and recovering the first stage.
Avellan and Scott Wisniewski, president of AST SpaceMobile, also did not get into specifics about financing the development of Blacklift. The company has already invested more than $1 billion in engines and will likely need billions more to develop and scale the vehicle.
Wisniewski said AST SpaceMobile plans to spend “several hundred million dollars” in 2027 on Blacklift development, but it is not clear whether that includes milestone payments to Firefly for propulsion. According to the company’s balance sheet, it had about $2.8 billion in unrestricted cash and cash equivalents at the end of September, and it has historically been successful in raising additional capital.
The company’s underlying business plan makes sense. There is a potentially very large market for space-to-ground connectivity for mobile devices. Traditional mobile service operators are growing wary about working with SpaceX, viewing the company as a competitor rather than a partner. And the recent issues with Starlink in Ukraine may lead some nations to seek alternative partners for these services.
“First of all, I’m no Musk, and I don’t want to be,” Avellan said on Thursday. “We partner. We don’t compete. We enhance. … Why? Because we partner with them. We don’t compete with them. We don’t insult them. You know, we partner with them.”
SpaceX went from being a rocket company to operating satellites. Now Avellan and AST seek to go from being a satellite operator to launching rockets. Consider that SpaceX took eight years from its founding to launch the Falcon 9, another five years to successfully land a booster, and several more years to achieve a high flight rate. AST is seeking to compress much of that process into approximately two years.
But rocket science is in no way simple, and the road ahead is sure to be rocky. Avellan said AST doesn’t really want to be in the launch business. Given how difficult, demanding, and expensive the launch business is, he may get his wish in a few years.

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with Gemini 4 Carbon in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Selecting Orchestrator from the model selector in Google Antigravity.
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.
Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business .

Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center, while Palestinian officials report at least six people killed, including a surgeon. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire.
Israel said it had targeted a senior Hamas member in a Gaza hospital in an overnight airstrike which reportedly killed six people.
According to the Israeli military, Muhammad Abu Ismail and other militants from the Islamist group had been operating a command center inside the Nasser hospital in Khan Yunis.
Gaza's civil defense service said at least six people were killed, including a surgeon and more than 20 were wounded. It said that parts of several floors were severely damaged or destroyed.
During war, hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law, although they can lose that protection if they are used for military purposes.
In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military (IDF) said, without providing evidence, that Hamas was "operating within Nasser Hospital in Khan Yunis" and were using the complex "as a hub for military and terrorist activities against IDF troops and Israel."
The IDF identified the targeted senior Hamas member as Abu Ismail, adding he "was responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war."
The IDF said the hospital was used for storing weapons, to conduct interrogation, operate command-and-control rooms as well as to shelter terrorists.
The Gaza Health Ministry said the Israeli airstrike hit the surgery department, killing six people including surgeon Rizk Abu Sharia.
News agency Reuters reported seeing footage from inside the hospital showing extensive damage with debris scattered around rooms and equipment.
Wounded people were also seen in the wreckage while several bodies were being carried away as firefighters worked to clear the scene.
Hamas has described the strike as a "fully-fledged war crime."
Since the beginning of the war in 2023, Israeli forces have attacked several hospitals in the Gaza Strip.
The war on Hamas in Gaza began in October 2023 after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel , killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Since then, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.
More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.
A ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, but attacks have continued since then. While Israel says Hamas is trying to regroup, the Palestinian militant group says it's committed to the ceasefire and that Israel is trying to undermine the agreement.
Hamas is recognized as a terrorist organization by the EU, the US and several Arab states.

An overnight Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians Thursday, including a teenage boy and a surgeon, medics said. Elsewhere in the devastated Palestinian territory, a nine-month-old baby died from the cold as families flee worsening flooding.
An Israeli air strike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the ravaged territory.
The strike hit a building containing surgery wards at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis. Israel 's ​military alleged it had ‌targeted a senior Hamas commander and accused the militants of using the hospital complex to plan attacks, which ⁠the group denied.
Medics and witnesses said two missiles crashed through the roof of the five-storey building, causing extensive damage. The surgery department, which serves half of Gaza's 2 million people, was knocked out of service. ‌Twenty others were wounded.
Ayman Abu Obeid, a doctor who was wounded in the attack, said he was on ⁠an overnight shift in the hospital when an explosion ripped through the room where he and others were sleeping.
"All of a sudden the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once," he said from a hospital bed. Near him, piles ​of mangled furniture and medical equipment could be seen covered in dust from blown-out concrete. Torn wires hung down ‌from the ceiling.
Among those killed was Rezik Abushira, a surgeon who was featured in a 2026 documentary, "American Doctor" , working alongside three visiting US doctors who help provide medical care for Palestinians in Gaza.
The dead also included a 13-year-old boy, according to Gaza's education ministry.
Three more Palestinians were killed later on Thursday in separate ‌incidents. Two were killed and several wounded in an Israeli airstrike on a car in Gaza City, and one other person was killed by Israeli gunfire in central Gaza's Bureij refugee camp, medics said, ​taking Thursday's death toll to at least nine.
Commenting on the vehicle strike, the Israeli military said it hit a Hamas militant without giving further details. It did not comment on the other incident.
In a statement on the hospital strike, Israel's ​military said it targeted a person named Muhammad Abu Ismail, describing him as "the commander of Hamas' Khan Younis Brigade". The military alleged he and other ​militants "were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital".
The military accused the militants of "turning the Nasser Hospital compound into a ​headquarters and operating from there".
Hamas rejected the military's claim that it had used the hospital as a base for operations. It did not immediately comment on whether a leader from the group had ​been targeted, wounded or killed in the strike.
The Board of Peace , the body placed in charge of overseeing Gaza's ceasefire plan by US President Donald Trump , on Thursday called for the peace plan's immediate implementation.
"The tragic loss of life following an Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis underscores precisely why President Trump's Comprehensive Peace Plan must be implemented immediately without further delay," the Board said in a statement.
Israel's military has struck the Nasser Hospital complex at least seven times since the start of the Gaza war, hospital officials say.
Heavy rain last week flooded tens of thousands of people's tents in the Palestinian territory , where virtually the whole population has been displaced at least once by three years of Israeli bombardment.
Five people, including three children, died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment collapsed onto their tents.
A nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on Thursday, his father and a doctor told AFP.
The doctor, who saw the child and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq "died from hypothermia inside his family's displacement tent" in Khan Younis.
Ahmed Raqiq told AFP that his son Kinan died of cold during the night in their tent in southern Gaza.
"I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death," he said.
"I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in burial shroud," he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet.

Hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and central and northern areas of the territory after they were inundated by rainwater.
James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN children's agency, UNICEF , warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season.
"It's very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It's not yet winter," Elder said.
"We're weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold."
The UN 's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms.
Around 65 percent of Gaza's people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said.
Israel and Hamas declared a ceasefire on October 10, 2025 but Israel has kept striking the territory, vowing to kill anyone involved in the Hamas-led October 7 attack , the deadliest in Israel's history.

Medical staff inspect damage to Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip on Thursday. Abdel Kareem Hana/AP hide caption
KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip — An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a general surgeon, and wounded at least 28 more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.
The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence.
The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgical wing and that a doctor, Rizk Abu Shaira, was among the dead. Inside the building, parts of several floors were either severely damaged or destroyed. Debris was scattered across hospital beds and equipment, and rebar dangled from the ceiling where the munition had penetrated.
British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.
"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department when the bomb hit. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.
He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," he said.
Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across Gaza, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. It has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.
In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.
In a statement on Thursday, the military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."
Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.
The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government but whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
Pictures showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics
The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.
In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.
Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.
The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded.
"What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said.
"Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."
Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts.
News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.
Photographs appeared to show an unexploded missile inside Nasser hospital's surgical building
Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion.
"My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC.
"I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."
He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg.
"Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."
He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."
Gaza's health ministry said surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira was among those killed
The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.
"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.
The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.
A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".
"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.
However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.
Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.
"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.
Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.
Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.
The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.
More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Hospital director says 28 wounded in attack on one of few remaining medical facilities in the strip
An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
The Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday saying in a statement it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there, without providing evidence.
The strike destroyed part of the surgery department, and caused extensive damage to several floors. Services were suspended in four departments: radiology, laboratories, surgical operations and inpatient surgical wards, according to Dr Ahmed al-Fara, hospital director.
The ceiling of one of the wards had caved in, while debris-covered beds lay next to medical instruments twisted from the force of the blast. In other rooms, piles of rubble and shattered concrete cluttered the floor and a hole was left in the floor, where the bomb penetrated the building.
Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist at Nasser medical complex, who was wounded in the attack, said: “The bombing caused thick smoke to fill the rooms and fires to break out, amid the groans of wounded and people’s screams. There were many casualties and blood everywhere … Most of us sustained injuries to our limbs, as well as shrapnel wounds in different parts of our bodies.”
Ubaid said the strike came at about 12.30am, without warning. “The patients in the department were all surgical patients waiting to undergo operations. The bombing happened at a time when they should have been asleep,” he said.
Among the dead was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had featured in American Doctor , a documentary about doctors operating in Gaza.
“Dr Rizk was in the American Doctor documentary operating and serving his people. He lost his life doing that, he lost his life because he was doing that,” Dr Thaer Ahmad, who also featured in the documentary, posted on X.
Abu Shaira was killed alongside one of his patients, on whom he had operated.
Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, after Israeli bombing made most of the strip’s facilities unusable . Last year Israel also struck the hospital, killing five journalists in a double-tap strike on a location often used by reporters for filming. In all, the hospital has been attacked seven times since the war on Gaza began.
The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using hospitals as command centres and to store weapons, an accusation the militant movement rejects. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed in Gaza, while Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since 7 October 2023, with at least 95 still in custody.
About 90% of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damage by Israeli bombing, systematic destruction UN experts called “medicide”.
Attacking healthcare facilities and staff is illegal under international humanitarian law, though these facilities can lose their protected status if they are used for military purposes.
There is an increased need for healthcare during the winter months in Gaza , where rains have displaced people from their tents and increased communicable diseases in crowded encampments.
Already, Nasser hospital is lacking about 80% of its essential medicines and medical supplies, said al-Fara, its director.
One of those killed in Thursday’s strike was Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, who was admitted to Nasser hospital on Monday after a piece of debris fell on his back while he was helping clear rubble from a friend’s home. He was scheduled for surgery at 10am on Thursday, and was meant to receive further treatment abroad.
“Seif was a young man in the prime of his life. He wanted to live, rebuild his home and start a normal life, free from problems and suffering … Seif was killed after already losing two of his brothers and his father. His mother has now lost three of her sons,” said his cousin Tareq Abu Hatab, 37.
Israel launched the war in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. At least 74,645 people have since been killed in Gaza and Israel has carried out a genocide in the strip, according to the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel continues to carry out airstrikes in Gaza, killing more than 1,600 people since the October 2025 “ceasefire”, according to the Gaza ministry of health.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, right, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, during their meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, Moscow, Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP hide caption
MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.
Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, second right, speaks to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, second left, and Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, third left, as Russian Presidential foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, behind Putin, and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Special Presidential Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries Kirill Dmitriev, right, sit near during the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, in Moscow, on Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP hide caption
But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.
Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.
Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.
He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference after a bilateral meeting with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Wednesday, ahead of the European Political Community Summit. Virginia Mayo/AP hide caption
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.
Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.
"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.
He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.
Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.
Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.
Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.
Law enforcement officer inspects the site of a car explosion that killed a military serviceman in St. Petersburg, Russia, Thursday. AP hide caption
A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

At least one person died after five people were shot early Thursday in a Washington, DC neighbourhood near the White House, police said. A swarm of officers responded to a nearby apartment building where a suspect was barricaded and later shot himself.
Five people were shot Thursday in a trendy Washington, DC neighbourhood within walking distance of the White House , police said, and a swarm of officers responded to a nearby apartment building where a suspect was barricaded.
The suspect, who later shot himself, is believed to have been in conflict with the building homeowners’ association.
At least one person shot at a gym died in a pool of blood, a witness said.
The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about 1 mile north of the White House . Police urged people to avoid the area of the 1500 block of 15th Street, which includes a VIDA fitness centre, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church and residences and is around the corner from a Whole Foods supermarket. Much of the block was cordoned off. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown.

Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building or on the ground below.
Authorities believe the suspect shot at least one person inside the gym before going outside and firing again, according to a law enforcement official who was not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.
Law enforcement agents believe the suspect shot another person in a parking garage elevator and then barricaded himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said.
James Spellman was at the gym a little after 8am when he heard shots being fired. He said there were about 50 people in the gym at the time.
“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”
Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym, and he said he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

Streets around the area also were blocked off during a massive police response. The federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said it sent agents to the scene to help. And the FBI said its Washington field office was helping local police with the investigation.
Witness Ryan Dubicki was in his nearby apartment around 8am when, he said, he “heard about five bangs”.
"They were really spread out so I thought it was construction,” he said. It was only a short time later that he looked out “and there were cops everywhere.”
His apartment building managers sent a notice that there was a possible active shooter.
The neighbourhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the Logan Circle neighbourhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.
Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime . That deployment continues today.

Police have apprehended a gunman who allegedly shot five people, killing one, in a busy thoroughfare in the centre of Washington, DC on Thursday morning.
Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll said the suspect, a white male, then barricaded himself inside a nearby apartment building. Police were negotiating with the suspect on the phone when they heard gunshots. Upon entering the room, they found the man had shot himself, Carrol said.
The shooting occurred on Thursday near Logan Circle, at the intersection of 15th Street NW and P Street, police said, at 8:23am local time (13:28 GMT).
Local and federal law enforcement, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Secret Service, cordoned off the area and worked to apprehend the suspected gunman, said Al Jazeera’s John Holman, reporting from the scene.
A witness told The Associated Press news agency he saw one person shot in the head inside a gym at the scene.
James Spellman was at the gym when he heard shots being fired. He said there were about 50 people there at the time.
“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”
Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym and he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.
The attack took place about 1.6km (one mile) from the White House during the rush hour commute.
Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown. Police issued a shelter-in-place order as law enforcement descended on the block.
“Go inside the nearest building, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until further notice,” police instructed the public. Trump’s focus on crime
The attack comes as the administration of United States President Donald Trump has made crime in the US capital a key issue during his second term.
That has included deploying the US National Guard across the city, a move Trump took after a former Department of Government Efficiency official said he was assaulted in the early hours of a morning in August 2025.
The US president declared a crime emergency, which also included federalising control of the federal district’s local police force.
Several thousand National Guard troops have remained in the district, with Trump regularly claiming their presence has brought down crime . Local officials have said the National Guard has not been used in local law enforcement.
The presence of the soldiers has at times caused friction with local officials, including Washington, DC mayor Muriel Bowser.
Speaking at a press conference alongside the police chief after the shooting, Bowser praised local police for their quick response to the incident, and dismissed the suggestion law enforcement had treated it with unusual importance.
“I praise [DC police] for bringing down crime in this city, and I praise our prosecutors,” Bowser said. “It’s not typical to have a active shooter that guns down people in the city, so all our law enforcement responded.”
The White House did not immediately comment on Thursday’s attack.
In November of last year, a National Guard member was killed by a gunman while on duty near 17th and I Streets NW. A second National Guard member was wounded.
In October, another National Guard member was shot during a gunfight in southeast Washington, DC.

US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.
A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.
In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".
Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.
He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads.
In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Hegseth (right) awarded the medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias after being reprimanded by him
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell later said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.
During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.
"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.
Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill .
Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a ‘violent attack’.
Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying for Tehran by a court in the United Kingdom after being accused of conducting surveillance on several people, including journalists for a Persian-language broadcaster in London.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted on Thursday following a six-week trial at Woolwich Crown Court in south London for engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service in a bid to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK .
These included journalists for Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. Iran International is banned by the government in Tehran.
A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted on all charges.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was outlawed by the UK in July under new powers to counteract state threats, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for anyone convicted of supporting or assisting the organisation.
“This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime,” Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, told reporters.
He said the pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while Sepahvand was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets.
London’s Metropolitan Police said this was the fourth case in recent years involving direct threats to Iranian journalists in the UK and that it is “working hard to keep them safe”.
“The threat from hostile states to the UK is increasing and Iran continues to adapt its approach to using ‘proxies’,” said Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner at the Met.
“We have seen examples where people who fly into the country to carry out criminal activity and then leave shortly afterwards, others where they use British nationals or, in this case, Iranian nationals with settled immigration status,” she added.
Most recently , Iran has been linked with a plot against a United States-run military airbase in England .
Sepahvand and Manesh were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.
The pair will be sentenced at London’s Central Criminal Court, better known as the Old Bailey, on December 17.

Russian president says he would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine and refuses to soften territorial demands
Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.
During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine , describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.
Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.
The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.
Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.
Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.
The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum , which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.
EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.
More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.
According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.
The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.
